$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy})=y{e}^{xy}, & \,\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy})=x{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}y{e}^{xy} & x{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}].

$$

the total derivative ${f}^{′}$ is given by 

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x} & \bbox[3pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}} & \frac{1}{z} \\ \bbox[3pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}} & {x}^{2}z & \bbox[3pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}}\end{aligned}].
$$

From left to right, what are the missing entries?" :question/worked-solution "Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂z}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{x},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{y},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{z} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}yz)=2xyz,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}yz)={x}^{2}z,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}yz)={x}^{2}y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x} & \frac{1}{y} & \frac{1}{z} \\ 2xyz & {x}^{2}z & {x}^{2}y\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186194429 :answer-field/correct "answer-f3204833-987c-5155-a299-7bcc45208ed9" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b28b947e-e099-5a84-a1f1-e49c76339f4d" "answer-f3204833-987c-5155-a299-7bcc45208ed9" "answer-ce8a1cde-3900-5ec2-8cba-bd78da711720" "answer-595978fe-cf25-5127-9b94-47cb53657dd6" "answer-52ae776e-08b3-54b7-a885-e9217261d1b0"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b28b947e-e099-5a84-a1f1-e49c76339f4d" :answer/id #uuid "b28b947e-e099-5a84-a1f1-e49c76339f4d" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$2xyz,\,$ $\frac{1}{y},\,$ and $yz$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f3204833-987c-5155-a299-7bcc45208ed9" :answer/id #uuid "f3204833-987c-5155-a299-7bcc45208ed9" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$2xyz,\,$ $\frac{1}{y},\,$ and ${x}^{2}y$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ce8a1cde-3900-5ec2-8cba-bd78da711720" :answer/id #uuid "ce8a1cde-3900-5ec2-8cba-bd78da711720" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$2xyz,\,$ $\frac{1}{z},\,$ and ${y}^{2}z$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-595978fe-cf25-5127-9b94-47cb53657dd6" :answer/id #uuid "595978fe-cf25-5127-9b94-47cb53657dd6" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "${x}^{2}y,\,$ $\frac{1}{x},\,$ and ${x}^{2}y$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-52ae776e-08b3-54b7-a885-e9217261d1b0" :answer/id #uuid "52ae776e-08b3-54b7-a885-e9217261d1b0" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "${x}^{2}y,\,$ $\frac{1}{z},\,$ and ${x}^{2}y$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198653 :question/problem "Consider the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

what is the sum of the missing values?" :question/worked-solution "Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}+y)={e}^{x},\, & \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}+y)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Evaluating $f$ and its derivative at $x=a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
f(a)=2,\,{f}^{′}(a)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The tangent to $f$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
z-f(a)={f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

Substituting $f(a),$ ${f}^{′}(a),$ and $a$ in the equation above, we obtain

$$
z-2=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]).
$$

Therefore, the sum of the missing values is

$$
2+1+1=4.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186194549 :answer-field/correct 17592186194553 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199487 :tutorial/content "We've spent some time studying so-called **plane transformations** of the form

$$
\mathbf T: \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2.
$$

In this lesson, we'll generalize our understanding of derivatives to transformations (or functions) of the form 

$$
\boldsymbol f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m.
$$

To motivate the discussion, we start by considering functions of one variable. 

Recall that a function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is **differentiable** at a point $x = a$ if there exists a number $f'(a)$, called the **derivative** of $f$ at $a$, such that

$$
f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}.
$$

We can restate this definition by applying basic algebraic properties of limits.

Since the left-hand side, $f'(a)$, is just a constant, we can rewrite the equation as

$$
\lim_{x \to a} f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a},
$$

using the fact that the limit of a constant is the constant itself.

Bringing all terms to one side, we obtain

$$
\lim_{x \to a} \left( \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a} - f'(a) \right) = 0,
$$

which can be rearranged as

$$
\lim_{x \to a} \left( \frac{f(x) - f(a) - f'(a)(x - a)}{x - a} \right) = 0.
$$

This final expression tells us that the difference between $f(x)$ and its *linear approximation* $f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$ becomes negligible relative to $x - a$ as $x$ approaches $a$.

In other words, not only does $f(x)$ become close to $f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$ near $a$, but the error between them shrinks *faster than* the distance $|x - a|$ itself.

Let's see how we can generalize this definition to vector-valued functions." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199495 :tutorial/content "Suppose that a transformation (or function) $\boldsymbol f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is defined by 

![](images/cd/cd9132d6a0e934349ae58a0718e6320cba3dd8ae84de7df2e3fb98b391256b57.svg) 

where $f_1,f_2,\ldots,f_m$ are scalar functions of $n$ variables. 
We say that $\boldsymbol{f}$ is **differentiable** at a point $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ if there exists an $m \times n$ matrix $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})$, called the **total derivative** of $\boldsymbol{f}$ at $\mathbf{a}$, such that

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{a}}
\frac{
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}) - \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{a}) - \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
}{
||\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}||
}
= \mathbf{0}.
$$

In other words, near $\mathbf{a}$, the function $\boldsymbol{f}$ is well-approximated by the linear map

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{a}) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}),
$$

and the error between $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})$ and this linear approximation becomes negligible compared to the distance $\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}\|$ as $\mathbf{x}$ approaches $\mathbf{a}$.

If $\boldsymbol{f}$ is differentiable at $\mathbf{x},$ then the total derivative of $\boldsymbol f$ is given by the matrix

![](images/6b/6bd7bcfb4e48c1833ff57c614bb18f469ca0a17e8a6e29d730b9e940c2f58984.svg)

Note the following:

- We sometimes refer to $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf x)$ simply as **the derivative** of $\boldsymbol f(\mathbf x).$

- For scalar-valued functions of the form $f: \mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R,$ the total derivative is the *transpose* of the gradient vector:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a) = \left(\nabla f \right)^T(\mathbf a)
$$

- For vector-valued functions $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ of a single parameter $t,$ the total derivative at $t=a$ is the usual column vector containing the partial derivatives of the components of $f{:}$
![](images/27/27651b3ca026cad63ee6cbbd88162d3ce85b9afc642986daf0ae76c6519bdc38.svg)

- For functions of the form $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2,$ the *determinant* of this matrix is the corresponding Jacobian: 

$$
\det\left(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)\right)  = \dfrac{\partial (f_1,f_2)}{\partial (x_1,x_2)}
$$

Similarly, for functions of the form $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3,$ the *determinant* of this matrix is the corresponding Jacobian: 

$$
\det\left(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)\right)  = \dfrac{\partial (f_1,f_2,f_3)}{\partial (x_1,x_2,x_3)}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199488 :tutorial/content "The equation of the tangent plane to a surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0),$ where $z_0=f(x_0,y_0),$ is given by

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0) \cdot \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0) \cdot \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

Let's express this equation in terms of the total derivative.

Writing our multivariable function $f:\mathbb R^2 \to \mathbb R$ as $f\left(\mathbf x \right),$ where ![](images/88/88f9f758bffba384670449973c5c89edae05c67268d2914a12801b21b60a319f.svg) the total derivative of $f$ is given by

![](images/56/56dc34676135e9c35b9e08cff732715c5d878d4a19f4fee6625384460ed6ee5f.svg)

Let ![](images/ca/ca5b0074c216a3235f015d7b96dece9ffc6fc50eecbdd0b5e97dfbd89eb446fa.svg) Then, we can re-write the equation of the tangent plane as a matrix equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-{z}_{0} & =(x-{x}_{0})\cdot \frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\cdot \frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) \\ z-{z}_{0} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) & \frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x-{x}_{0} \\ y-{y}_{0}\end{aligned}] \\ z-f({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) & \frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\end{aligned}]\cdot ([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}{x}_{0} \\ {y}_{0}\end{aligned}]) \\ z-f(a) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(a) & \frac{∂f}{∂y}(a)\end{aligned}]\cdot (x-a) \\ z-f(a) & ={f}^{′}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane to $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ at $\mathbf x = \mathbf{a},$ in matrix form, is given by

$$
z - f(\mathbf a) = \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)(\mathbf x - \mathbf a).
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199489 :tutorial/content "If $f:\mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ is differentiable at $x=a,$ then for points close to $x=a,$ we have the linear approximation

$$
f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x-a).
$$

We have a similar result for transformations of the form $\boldsymbol{f}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m.$

If $\boldsymbol f:\mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^m$ is differentiable at $\mathbf x=\mathbf a,$ then for points close to $\mathbf x=\mathbf a,$ we have the linear approximation

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf x) \approx \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf a) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)(\mathbf x - \mathbf a).
$$

 

Notice that this approximation for $\boldsymbol f$ is affine. Thus, if a function is differentiable at a point $\mathbf x = \mathbf a,$ it is **locally affine** in a neighborhood of $\mathbf x = \mathbf a.$ 

Let's see some examples." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198497 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

From left to right, what are the missing entries?" :question/worked-solution "Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂z}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{x},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{y},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{z} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}yz)=2xyz,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}yz)={x}^{2}z,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}yz)={x}^{2}y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x} & \frac{1}{y} & \frac{1}{z} \\ 2xyz & {x}^{2}z & {x}^{2}y\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186194429 :answer-field/correct "answer-f3204833-987c-5155-a299-7bcc45208ed9" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b28b947e-e099-5a84-a1f1-e49c76339f4d" "answer-f3204833-987c-5155-a299-7bcc45208ed9" "answer-ce8a1cde-3900-5ec2-8cba-bd78da711720" "answer-595978fe-cf25-5127-9b94-47cb53657dd6" "answer-52ae776e-08b3-54b7-a885-e9217261d1b0"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b28b947e-e099-5a84-a1f1-e49c76339f4d" :answer/id #uuid "b28b947e-e099-5a84-a1f1-e49c76339f4d" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$2xyz,\,$ $\frac{1}{y},\,$ and $yz$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f3204833-987c-5155-a299-7bcc45208ed9" :answer/id #uuid "f3204833-987c-5155-a299-7bcc45208ed9" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$2xyz,\,$ $\frac{1}{y},\,$ and ${x}^{2}y$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ce8a1cde-3900-5ec2-8cba-bd78da711720" :answer/id #uuid "ce8a1cde-3900-5ec2-8cba-bd78da711720" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$2xyz,\,$ $\frac{1}{z},\,$ and ${y}^{2}z$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-595978fe-cf25-5127-9b94-47cb53657dd6" :answer/id #uuid "595978fe-cf25-5127-9b94-47cb53657dd6" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "${x}^{2}y,\,$ $\frac{1}{x},\,$ and ${x}^{2}y$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-52ae776e-08b3-54b7-a885-e9217261d1b0" :answer/id #uuid "52ae776e-08b3-54b7-a885-e9217261d1b0" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "${x}^{2}y,\,$ $\frac{1}{z},\,$ and ${x}^{2}y$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198653 :question/problem "Consider the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

what is the sum of the missing values?" :question/worked-solution "Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}+y)={e}^{x},\, & \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}+y)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Evaluating $f$ and its derivative at $x=a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
f(a)=2,\,{f}^{′}(a)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The tangent to $f$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
z-f(a)={f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

Substituting $f(a),$ ${f}^{′}(a),$ and $a$ in the equation above, we obtain

$$
z-2=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]).
$$

Therefore, the sum of the missing values is

$$
2+1+1=4.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186194549 :answer-field/correct 17592186194553 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199487 :tutorial/content "We've spent some time studying so-called **plane transformations** of the form

$$
\mathbf T: \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2.
$$

In this lesson, we'll generalize our understanding of derivatives to transformations (or functions) of the form 

$$
\boldsymbol f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m.
$$

To motivate the discussion, we start by considering functions of one variable. 

Recall that a function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is **differentiable** at a point $x = a$ if there exists a number $f'(a)$, called the **derivative** of $f$ at $a$, such that

$$
f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}.
$$

We can restate this definition by applying basic algebraic properties of limits.

Since the left-hand side, $f'(a)$, is just a constant, we can rewrite the equation as

$$
\lim_{x \to a} f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a},
$$

using the fact that the limit of a constant is the constant itself.

Bringing all terms to one side, we obtain

$$
\lim_{x \to a} \left( \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a} - f'(a) \right) = 0,
$$

which can be rearranged as

$$
\lim_{x \to a} \left( \frac{f(x) - f(a) - f'(a)(x - a)}{x - a} \right) = 0.
$$

This final expression tells us that the difference between $f(x)$ and its *linear approximation* $f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$ becomes negligible relative to $x - a$ as $x$ approaches $a$.

In other words, not only does $f(x)$ become close to $f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$ near $a$, but the error between them shrinks *faster than* the distance $|x - a|$ itself.

Let's see how we can generalize this definition to vector-valued functions." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199495 :tutorial/content "Suppose that a transformation (or function) $\boldsymbol f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is defined by 

![](images/cd/cd9132d6a0e934349ae58a0718e6320cba3dd8ae84de7df2e3fb98b391256b57.svg) 

where $f_1,f_2,\ldots,f_m$ are scalar functions of $n$ variables. 
We say that $\boldsymbol{f}$ is **differentiable** at a point $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ if there exists an $m \times n$ matrix $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})$, called the **total derivative** of $\boldsymbol{f}$ at $\mathbf{a}$, such that

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{a}}
\frac{
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}) - \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{a}) - \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
}{
||\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}||
}
= \mathbf{0}.
$$

In other words, near $\mathbf{a}$, the function $\boldsymbol{f}$ is well-approximated by the linear map

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{a}) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}),
$$

and the error between $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})$ and this linear approximation becomes negligible compared to the distance $\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}\|$ as $\mathbf{x}$ approaches $\mathbf{a}$.

If $\boldsymbol{f}$ is differentiable at $\mathbf{x},$ then the total derivative of $\boldsymbol f$ is given by the matrix

![](images/6b/6bd7bcfb4e48c1833ff57c614bb18f469ca0a17e8a6e29d730b9e940c2f58984.svg)

Note the following:

- We sometimes refer to $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf x)$ simply as **the derivative** of $\boldsymbol f(\mathbf x).$

- For scalar-valued functions of the form $f: \mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R,$ the total derivative is the *transpose* of the gradient vector:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a) = \left(\nabla f \right)^T(\mathbf a)
$$

- For vector-valued functions $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ of a single parameter $t,$ the total derivative at $t=a$ is the usual column vector containing the partial derivatives of the components of $f{:}$
![](images/27/27651b3ca026cad63ee6cbbd88162d3ce85b9afc642986daf0ae76c6519bdc38.svg)

- For functions of the form $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2,$ the *determinant* of this matrix is the corresponding Jacobian: 

$$
\det\left(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)\right)  = \dfrac{\partial (f_1,f_2)}{\partial (x_1,x_2)}
$$

Similarly, for functions of the form $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3,$ the *determinant* of this matrix is the corresponding Jacobian: 

$$
\det\left(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)\right)  = \dfrac{\partial (f_1,f_2,f_3)}{\partial (x_1,x_2,x_3)}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199488 :tutorial/content "The equation of the tangent plane to a surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0),$ where $z_0=f(x_0,y_0),$ is given by

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0) \cdot \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0) \cdot \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

Let's express this equation in terms of the total derivative.

Writing our multivariable function $f:\mathbb R^2 \to \mathbb R$ as $f\left(\mathbf x \right),$ where ![](images/88/88f9f758bffba384670449973c5c89edae05c67268d2914a12801b21b60a319f.svg) the total derivative of $f$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}z-{z}_{0} & =(x-{x}_{0})\cdot \frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\cdot \frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) \\ z-{z}_{0} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) & \frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x-{x}_{0} \\ y-{y}_{0}\end{aligned}] \\ z-f({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) & \frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\end{aligned}]\cdot ([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}{x}_{0} \\ {y}_{0}\end{aligned}]) \\ z-f(a) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(a) & \frac{∂f}{∂y}(a)\end{aligned}]\cdot (x-a) \\ z-f(a) & ={f}^{′}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}

Therefore, the tangent plane to $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ at $\mathbf x = \mathbf{a},$ in matrix form, is given by

$$
z - f(\mathbf a) = \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)(\mathbf x - \mathbf a).
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199489 :tutorial/content "If $f:\mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ is differentiable at $x=a,$ then for points close to $x=a,$ we have the linear approximation

$$
f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x-a).

We have a similar result for transformations of the form $\boldsymbol{f}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m.$

$$
\mathbf T: \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2.
$$

In this lesson, we'll generalize our understanding of derivatives to transformations (or functions) of the form 

$$
\boldsymbol f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m.
$$

To motivate the discussion, we start by considering functions of one variable. 

Recall that a function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is **differentiable** at a point $x = a$ if there exists a number $f'(a)$, called the **derivative** of $f$ at $a$, such that

$$
f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}.
$$

We can restate this definition by applying basic algebraic properties of limits.

Since the left-hand side, $f'(a)$, is just a constant, we can rewrite the equation as

$$
\lim_{x \to a} f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a},
$$

using the fact that the limit of a constant is the constant itself.

Bringing all terms to one side, we obtain

$$
\lim_{x \to a} \left( \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a} - f'(a) \right) = 0,
$$

which can be rearranged as

$$
\lim_{x \to a} \left( \frac{f(x) - f(a) - f'(a)(x - a)}{x - a} \right) = 0.
$$

This final expression tells us that the difference between $f(x)$ and its *linear approximation* $f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$ becomes negligible relative to $x - a$ as $x$ approaches $a$.

In other words, not only does $f(x)$ become close to $f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$ near $a$, but the error between them shrinks *faster than* the distance $|x - a|$ itself.

Let's see how we can generalize this definition to vector-valued functions."] [17592186199495 :tutorial/content "Suppose that a transformation (or function) $\boldsymbol f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is defined by 

![](images/cd/cd9132d6a0e934349ae58a0718e6320cba3dd8ae84de7df2e3fb98b391256b57.svg) 

where $f_1,f_2,\ldots,f_m$ are scalar functions of $n$ variables. 
We say that $\boldsymbol{f}$ is **differentiable** at a point $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ if there exists an $m \times n$ matrix $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})$, called the **total derivative** of $\boldsymbol{f}$ at $\mathbf{a}$, such that

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{a}}
\frac{
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}) - \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{a}) - \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
}{
||\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}||
}
= \mathbf{0}.
$$

In other words, near $\mathbf{a}$, the function $\boldsymbol{f}$ is well-approximated by the linear map

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{a}) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}),
$$

and the error between $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})$ and this linear approximation becomes negligible compared to the distance $\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}\|$ as $\mathbf{x}$ approaches $\mathbf{a}$.

If $\boldsymbol{f}$ is differentiable at $\mathbf{x},$ then the total derivative of $\boldsymbol f$ is given by the matrix

![](images/6b/6bd7bcfb4e48c1833ff57c614bb18f469ca0a17e8a6e29d730b9e940c2f58984.svg)

Note the following:

- We sometimes refer to $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf x)$ simply as **the derivative** of $\boldsymbol f(\mathbf x).$

- For scalar-valued functions of the form $f: \mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R,$ the total derivative is the *transpose* of the gradient vector:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a) = \left(\nabla f \right)^T(\mathbf a)
$$

- For vector-valued functions $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ of a single parameter $t,$ the total derivative at $t=a$ is the usual column vector containing the partial derivatives of the components of $f{:}$
![](images/27/27651b3ca026cad63ee6cbbd88162d3ce85b9afc642986daf0ae76c6519bdc38.svg)

- For functions of the form $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2,$ the *determinant* of this matrix is the corresponding Jacobian: 

$$
\det\left(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)\right)  = \dfrac{\partial (f_1,f_2)}{\partial (x_1,x_2)}
$$

Similarly, for functions of the form $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3,$ the *determinant* of this matrix is the corresponding Jacobian: 

$$
\det\left(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)\right)  = \dfrac{\partial (f_1,f_2,f_3)}{\partial (x_1,x_2,x_3)}
$$"] [17592186199488 :tutorial/content "The equation of the tangent plane to a surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0),$ where $z_0=f(x_0,y_0),$ is given by

In this lesson, we'll generalize our understanding of derivatives to transformations (or functions) of the form

$$\boldsymbol f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m.$$

To motivate the discussion, we start by considering functions of one variable.

Recall that a function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is **differentiable** at a point $x = a$ if there exists a number $f'(a)$, called the **derivative** of $f$ at $a$, such that

$$f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}.$$

We can restate this definition by applying basic algebraic properties of limits.

Since the left-hand side, $f'(a)$, is just a constant, we can rewrite the equation as

$$\lim_{x \to a} f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a},$$

using the fact that the limit of a constant is the constant itself.

Bringing all terms to one side, we obtain

$$\lim_{x \to a} \left( \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a} - f'(a) \right) = 0,$$

which can be rearranged as

$$\lim_{x \to a} \left( \frac{f(x) - f(a) - f'(a)(x - a)}{x - a} \right) = 0.$$

This final expression tells us that the difference between $f(x)$ and its *linear approximation* $f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$ becomes negligible relative to $x - a$ as $x$ approaches $a$.

In other words, not only does $f(x)$ become close to $f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$ near $a$, but the error between them shrinks *faster than* the distance $|x - a|$ itself.

f(x)=x{y}^{2}-y,\,x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}],

calculate ${f}^{′}$ at $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-y)={y}^{2}, & \,\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-y)=2xy-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & 2xy-1\end{aligned}]
$$

and ${f}^{′}$ at $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ is

$$
{f}^{′}(a)=[\begin{aligned}(1)^{2} & 2(0)(1)-1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186389381 :question/id #uuid "64d550f1-8d2f-5aa7-8e7b-a4c907c4afdf" :question/math-academy-id "q-163032"} {:db/id 17592186389388 :question/id #uuid From left to right, what are the missing entries?" :question/worked-solution "Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂z}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xyz})=yz{e}^{xyz},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xyz})=xz{e}^{xyz},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{xyz})=xy{e}^{xyz} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+yz)=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+yz)=z,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(x+yz)=y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}yz{e}^{xyz} & xz{e}^{xyz} & xy{e}^{xyz} \\ 1 & z & y\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198413 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198055 :question/id #uuid "db0be438-94fe-52de-9daf-60d1727ce7b9" :question/math-academy-id "e-12479"} :knowledge-point/id :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{xy+1},\,x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].
$$

If the tangent to $f$ at $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is given by

$$
z-∗=[\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])
$$

what is the sum of the missing values?" :question/worked-solution "Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{xy+1})=-\frac{y}{(xy+1)^{2}},\, & \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{xy+1})=-\frac{x}{(xy+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{y}{(xy+1)^{2}} & -\frac{x}{(xy+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Evaluating $f$ and its derivative at $x=a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
f(a)=\frac{1}{2},\,{f}^{′}(a)=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{4} & -\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}].
$$

The tangent to $f$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
z-f(a)={f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

Substituting $f(a),$ ${f}^{′}(a),$ and $a$ in the equation above, we obtain

$$
z-\frac{1}{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{4} & -\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]).
$$

Therefore, the sum of the missing values is

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the transformation $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2},$ defined as

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

If the linear approximation of $f$ at  $a=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\pi }{2} \\ \frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}]$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈[\begin{aligned}\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4} \\ ∗\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & ∗ \\ ∗ & -1\end{aligned}](x-[\begin{aligned}\frac{\pi }{2} \\ \frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}]),

what is the sum of the missing values?" :question/worked-solution "Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2})=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2})=2{x}_{2} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}))=\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}))=\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2{x}_{2} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \operatorname{cos}⁡({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})\end{aligned}].
$$

Evaluating $f$ and its derivative at $x=a=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\pi }{2} \\ \frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
f(a)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{f}^{′}(a)=[\begin{aligned}1 & \pi  \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The linear approximation of $f$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

Substituting $f(a),$ ${f}^{′}(a),$ and $a$ in the equation above, we obtain

$$
f(x)≈[\begin{aligned}\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & \pi  \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}](x-[\begin{aligned}\frac{\pi }{2} \\ \frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}]).
$$

Therefore, the sum of the missing values is

$$
0+\pi +(-1)=\pi -1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367818 :question/id #uuid "0b2db507-0842-5c58-a0f3-e75d325f34c4" :question/math-academy-id "q-163114"} {:db/id 17592186367832 :question/id #uuid "b78101c4-fecc-5cba-9eee-2c628a3b3929" :question/math-academy-id "q-163162" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198414 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9f09fc28-bdce-554f-98f5-019d34542a13" :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Affine Approximation of a Vector Function"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2bc8f2d1-ecfb-50d7-b14b-04f9786d82ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186367834} {:answer/id #uuid "5f7d0746-3536-5992-9206-08d262d180df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186367835} {:answer/id #uuid "64ad6963-dfe5-5f16-bbef-d203883d7998" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186367836} {:answer/id #uuid "566980c0-9d00-5a29-b05a-cac367edfbb2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186367837} {:answer/id #uuid "dc697d16-cd1d-50e1-81a4-0a7ea90187b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186367838}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "64ad6963-dfe5-5f16-bbef-d203883d7998" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186367836} :answer-field/id #uuid "703aea1e-c64a-581f-b4f6-a53c00907653" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186367833}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the transformation $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2},$ defined as

$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}]

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}^{3}-{x}_{2})=3{x}_{1}^{2},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}^{3}-{x}_{2})=-1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}{e}^{{x}_{1}})={x}_{2}{e}^{{x}_{1}},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}{e}^{{x}_{1}})={e}^{{x}_{1}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}^{2} & -1 \\ {x}_{2}{e}^{{x}_{1}} & {e}^{{x}_{1}}\end{aligned}].

$$

[{:db/id 17592186199335 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199487 :tutorial/content "We've spent some time studying so-called **plane transformations** of the form

$$\mathbf T: \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2.$$

In this lesson, we'll generalize our understanding of derivatives to transformations (or functions) of the form

$$\boldsymbol f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m.$$

To motivate the discussion, we start by considering functions of one variable.

Recall that a function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is **differentiable** at a point $x = a$ if there exists a number $f'(a)$, called the **derivative** of $f$ at $a$, such that

$$f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}.$$

We can restate this definition by applying basic algebraic properties of limits.

Since the left-hand side, $f'(a)$, is just a constant, we can rewrite the equation as

$$\lim_{x \to a} f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a},$$

using the fact that the limit of a constant is the constant itself.

Bringing all terms to one side, we obtain

$$\lim_{x \to a} \left( \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a} - f'(a) \right) = 0,$$

which can be rearranged as

$$\lim_{x \to a} \left( \frac{f(x) - f(a) - f'(a)(x - a)}{x - a} \right) = 0.$$

This final expression tells us that the difference between $f(x)$ and its *linear approximation* $f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$ becomes negligible relative to $x - a$ as $x$ approaches $a$.

In other words, not only does $f(x)$ become close to $f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$ near $a$, but the error between them shrinks *faster than* the distance $|x - a|$ itself.

Let's see how we can generalize this definition to vector-valued functions." :tutorial/id #uuid "a9769637-9fcb-5829-817e-f82930d6d99b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7762 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} the tangent plane to a surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0),$ where $z_0=f(x_0,y_0),$ is given by

$$z - z_0 = (x-x_0) \cdot \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0) \cdot \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).$$

Let's express this equation in terms of the total derivative.

Writing our multivariable function $f:\mathbb R^2 \to \mathbb R$ as $f\left(\mathbf x \right),$ where $\mathbf{x} = [\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}],$ the total derivative of $f$ is given by

$$\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf x) = [\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}].$$

Let $\mathbf{a} = [\begin{aligned}{x}_{0} \\ {y}_{0}\end{aligned}].$ Then, we can re-write the equation of the tangent plane as a matrix equation as follows:

$$\boldsymbol f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}] \longrightarrow [\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],$$

where $f_1,f_2,\ldots,f_m$ are scalar functions of $n$ variables. We say that $\boldsymbol{f}$ is **differentiable** at a point $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ if there exists an $m \times n$ matrix $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})$, called the **total derivative** of $\boldsymbol{f}$ at $\mathbf{a}$, such that

$$\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{a}} \frac{ \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}) - \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{a}) - \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) }{ ||\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}|| } = \mathbf{0}.$$

In other words, near $\mathbf{a}$, the function $\boldsymbol{f}$ is well-approximated by the linear map

$$\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{a}) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}),$$

and the error between $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})$ and this linear approximation becomes negligible compared to the distance $\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}\|$ as $\mathbf{x}$ approaches $\mathbf{a}$.

$$\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf x) = [\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].$$

$$\mathbf T: \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2.$$

In this lesson, we'll generalize our understanding of derivatives to transformations (or functions) of the form

$$\boldsymbol f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m.$$

To motivate the discussion, we start by considering functions of one variable.

Recall that a function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is **differentiable** at a point $x = a$ if there exists a number $f'(a)$, called the **derivative** of $f$ at $a$, such that

$$f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}.$$

We can restate this definition by applying basic algebraic properties of limits.

Since the left-hand side, $f'(a)$, is just a constant, we can rewrite the equation as

$$\lim_{x \to a} f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a},$$

using the fact that the limit of a constant is the constant itself.

Bringing all terms to one side, we obtain

$$\lim_{x \to a} \left( \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a} - f'(a) \right) = 0,$$

which can be rearranged as

$$\lim_{x \to a} \left( \frac{f(x) - f(a) - f'(a)(x - a)}{x - a} \right) = 0.$$

This final expression tells us that the difference between $f(x)$ and its *linear approximation* $f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$ becomes negligible relative to $x - a$ as $x$ approaches $a$.

In other words, not only does $f(x)$ become close to $f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$ near $a$, but the error between them shrinks *faster than* the distance $|x - a|$ itself.

Let's see how we can generalize this definition to vector-valued functions." :tutorial/id #uuid "a9769637-9fcb-5829-817e-f82930d6d99b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7762 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "087cad91-5bec-5130-91c0-60421a04d402" :step/math-academy-id 44919 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199362}} {:db/id 17592186199487 :tutorial/content "We've spent some time studying so-called **plane transformations** of the form

Notice that this approximation for $\boldsymbol f$ is affine. Thus, if a function is differentiable at a point $\mathbf x = \mathbf a,$ it is **locally affine** in a neighborhood of $\mathbf x = \mathbf a.$

Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "4f9fb273-0149-5dca-a967-7bb027abab86" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7765 :tutorial/title "Affine Approximations of Vector Functions"} {:db/id 17592186199495 :tutorial/content "Suppose that a transformation (or function) $\boldsymbol f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is defined by

$$\boldsymbol f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}] \longrightarrow [\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],$$

where $f_1,f_2,\ldots,f_m$ are scalar functions of $n$ variables. We say that $\boldsymbol{f}$ is **differentiable** at a point $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ if there exists an $m \times n$ matrix $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})$, called the **total derivative** of $\boldsymbol{f}$ at $\mathbf{a}$, such that

$$\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{a}} \frac{ \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}) - \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{a}) - \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) }{ ||\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}|| } = \mathbf{0}.$$

In other words, near $\mathbf{a}$, the function $\boldsymbol{f}$ is well-approximated by the linear map

$$\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{a}) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}),$$

and the error between $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})$ and this linear approximation becomes negligible compared to the distance $\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}\|$ as $\mathbf{x}$ approaches $\mathbf{a}$.

If $\boldsymbol{f}$ is differentiable at $\mathbf{x},$ then the total derivative of $\boldsymbol f$ is given by the matrix

$$\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf x) = [\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].$$

Note the following:

- We sometimes refer to $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf x)$ simply as **the derivative** of $\boldsymbol f(\mathbf x).$
- For scalar-valued functions of the form $f: \mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R,$ the total derivative is the *transpose* of the gradient vector: $$\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a) = \left(\nabla f \right)^T(\mathbf a)$$
- For vector-valued functions $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ of a single parameter $t,$ the total derivative at $t=a$ is the usual column vector containing the partial derivatives of the components of $f{:}$ $$\boldsymbol{f}'(a) = \left.[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂t} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂t} \\ ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{n}}{∂t}\end{aligned}]\right._{t = a }$$

- For functions of the form $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2,$ the *determinant* of this matrix is the corresponding Jacobian: $$\det\left(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)\right) = \dfrac{\partial (f_1,f_2)}{\partial (x_1,x_2)}$$ Similarly, for functions of the form $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3,$ the *determinant* of this matrix is the corresponding Jacobian: $$\det\left(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)\right) = \dfrac{\partial (f_1,f_2,f_3)}{\partial (x_1,x_2,x_3)}$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fb0be5f3-0f3d-5c1f-81f5-97faa1864dc1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7793 Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in
